cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Hi Thomas, how are you enjoying the course so far?

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Yeah, I think it’s good.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Remind me – why did you decide to study sports science? Didn’t you want to be a professional athlete when you were at school?

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Yeah – that was my goal, and all my classmates assumed I would achieve it; they thought I was brilliant. (Q21/22)

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: That must have been a nice feeling.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Mm, I thought I could win anything. There was no one who could run faster than me.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Exactly – so what happened? Did your mum and dad want you to be more ‘academic’?

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Not at all. Perhaps they should have pushed me harder, though. (Q21/22)

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: What do you mean?

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: I think I should have practised more.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: What makes you say that?

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Well, I went out to Kenya for a couple of weeks to train …

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Really! I didn’t know that.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: I was chosen to go there out of loads of kids and run with some of the top teenage athletes in the world. And … I was so calm about it. I just kept thinking how fortunate I was. What a great chance this was (Q23/24)! Everyone back home was so proud of me. But once we started competing, I very quickly realised I wasn’t good enough.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: That must have been a huge shock.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: I thought ‘this can’t be happening’ (Q23/24)! I was used to winning.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: I’m sorry to hear that.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: It’s OK. I’m over it now and I think it’s much better to do a university course and this one has such a variety of sports-related areas. It’s going to be good.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Oh, I agree – I chose it because of that.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: So Jeanne – have you thought of any ideas for the discussion session next week on technology and sport?

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: We have to cover more than one sport, don’t we?

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Yeah.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: You know – we always think technology is about the future, but we could gather some ideas about past developments in sport.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Look at early types of equipment perhaps? Uh, I remember reading something about table tennis bats once – how they ended up being covered with pimpled rubber.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Cos they were just wooden at first, I’d imagine.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Yeah. In about the 1920s, a factory was making rolls of the rubber in bulk (Q25) for something like horse harnesses.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Really!

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Yeah – and someone realised that it’d make a perfect covering for the wooden bats.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: So what about cricket – that’s had a few innovative changes. Maybe the pads they were on their legs?

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: I don’t think they’ve changed much but, I’m just looking on the internet … and it says that when the first cricket helmet came in, in 1978, the Australian batsman who first wore it was booed and jeered by people (Q26) watching because it was so ugly!

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Wow, players have to protect themselves from getting hurt! I mean everyone wears one now.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Mm, unlike the cycle helmet.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Well, unless you’re a professional, but you’re right, many ordinary bikers don’t wear a helmet.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Hey, look at these pictures of original helmet designs. This one looks like an upside-down bowl!

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Yet, the woman’s laughing – she’s so proud to be wearing it!

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: It says serious cyclists ended up with wet hair (Q27) from all the hard exercise.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: I guess that’s why they have large air vents in them now so that the skin can breathe more easily.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: OK, so we’ve done helmets. What about golf balls or better still golf clubs – they’ve changed a lot.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Yeah – I remember my great grandfather telling me that because a club was made entirely of wood, it would easily break and players had to get another. (Q28)

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: There’s no wood at all in them now, is there?

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: No – they’re much more powerful.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: The same must be true of hockey sticks.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: I don’t think so because players still use wooden sticks today. What it does say here, though, is that when the game started you had to produce a stick yourself. (Q29)

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: I guess they just weren’t being manufactured. So, one more perhaps. What about football?

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Well, I know the first balls were made of animal skin.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Yeah, they covered them with pieces of leather that were stitched together, but … the balls let in water when it rained.

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: Oh, that would have made them much heavier.

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: That’s right. You can imagine the damage to player’s necks when the ball was headed. (Q30)

cues.speaker: JEANNE
cues.text: How painful that must have been!

cues.speaker: THOMAS
cues.text: Yeah, well, I think we can put together some useful ideas …
